title: Ordering and Calculating with Decimals
summary: Compare and order positive and negative decimals and fractions with =, ≠, >, <, ≤ and ≥, then estimate and multiply decimals by decimals and divide by numbers with one decimal place.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand how big decimals and fractions are — including **negative** ones — so you can compare and order them, and use the symbols =, ≠, >, <, ≤ and ≥ correctly (8Nf.06)
Estimate, then multiply decimals by whole numbers and by other decimals, e.g. 2.7 × 6, 0.4 × 0.03 and 3.6 × 1.25 (8Nf.07)
Estimate, then divide decimals by numbers with **one decimal place**, e.g. 7.56 ÷ 0.6 and 18 ÷ 0.4 (8Nf.08)

blocks.text: In Stage 6 and 7 you added, subtracted, multiplied and divided decimals by whole numbers. In Stage 8 you go further: you compare negative decimals and fractions, you multiply a decimal by another decimal, and you divide by a decimal such as 0.6. The written methods are the ones you already know — the new skill is **knowing where the decimal point goes** and **checking with an estimate**.
Key words

items: decimal place (d.p.)
خانة عشرية — a digit after the decimal point; 3.45 has 2 decimal places
tenth, hundredth, thousandth
جزء من عشرة / من مئة / من ألف — 0.1, 0.01, 0.001
negative number
عدد سالب — a number less than zero, e.g. −0.6
compare / order
يقارن / يرتب — decide which is bigger; put numbers from smallest to largest (ascending) or largest to smallest (descending)
inequality symbols
رموز المتباينة — > greater than, < less than, ≥ greater than or equal to, ≤ less than or equal to, ≠ not equal to
estimate
تقدير — a quick rough answer using rounded numbers
product
حاصل الضرب — the answer to a multiplication
quotient
خارج القسمة — the answer to a division
divisor
المقسوم عليه — the number you divide by (in 7.56 ÷ 0.6 the divisor is 0.6)

blocks.text: 1. Comparing and ordering decimals

**Positive decimals.** Compare digit by digit from the left, place by place. It helps to give every number the same number of decimal places by writing zeros on the end — this does not change the value.

headers: Look at the first different digit

blocks.text: **Negative decimals.** Think of a number line: numbers get **smaller as you move left**. −0.6 is closer to zero than −0.75, so −0.6 is the bigger number. A quick rule: for two negative numbers, the one that looks 'bigger' without its minus sign is actually **smaller**. Any positive number is bigger than any negative number.

blocks.text: **Fractions and decimals together.** Change every fraction to a decimal (divide the numerator by the denominator), then compare the decimals. Learn the common ones by heart:
For harder fractions, divide: 5/6 = 5 ÷ 6 = 0.8333…  and  7/9 = 7 ÷ 9 = 0.777… Write enough decimal places to see the difference (at least 3).
2. The six symbols

rows: is greater than or equal to
is less than or equal to

blocks.text: The symbol always **opens towards the bigger number** (the 'mouth' eats the bigger one). Remember that ≥ and ≤ are true when the two numbers are equal, but > and < are **false** when they are equal: 0.75 ≤ 3/4 is true, but 0.75 < 3/4 is false. Also note 0.3 ≠ 1/3, because 1/3 = 0.333…

blocks.title: الأعداد السالبة
blocks.text: في الأعداد السالبة: كل ما الرقم يبعد عن الصفر ناحية الشمال يبقى أصغر. يعني −0.75 أصغر من −0.6، مع إن 75 أكبر من 6. ارسم خط أعداد صغير في ورقة الامتحان لو اتلخبطت، وحوّل الكسور لعشري قبل المقارنة.
3. Multiplying decimals
**Method — 'ignore the points, then put them back':**

items: **Estimate** by rounding each number (often to 1 significant figure).
Remove the decimal points and multiply the whole numbers (use any method: grid, column).
**Count** the decimal places in the question — add the counts for both numbers.
Your answer has **the same number of decimal places**. Count them from the right; write extra zeros at the front if you need them.
Only now remove any zeros at the end (4.500 = 4.5). Compare with your estimate.

blocks.text: **Why does it work?** 0.3 = 3 tenths and 0.4 = 4 tenths. Tenths × tenths = hundredths, so 0.3 × 0.4 = 12 hundredths = 0.12. The diagram shows it as an area.

blocks.text: **Big idea:** multiplying by a number **between 0 and 1 makes the answer smaller** (8 × 0.4 = 3.2, which is less than 8). Multiplying by a number bigger than 1 makes it bigger. Use this to check your answer is sensible.

**Using a known fact.** If you know 23 × 47 = 1081, you can write many related answers without calculating again — just count decimal places: 2.3 × 4.7 = 10.81 (2 d.p.), 0.23 × 47 = 10.81, 2.3 × 0.47 = 1.081 (3 d.p.), 230 × 4.7 = 1081 (the zero and the decimal place cancel out).
4. Dividing by a decimal with one decimal place

Dividing by a decimal like 0.6 is awkward. The trick: **multiply both numbers by 10** so the divisor becomes a whole number. The answer does not change, because a division is like a fraction and 7.56/0.6 = 75.6/6 (equivalent fractions).

items: **Estimate** using friendly numbers, e.g. 7.56 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 7.2 ÷ 0.6 = 12.
Multiply **both** the number and the divisor by 10 (move each decimal point one place right).
Do the division by a whole number (short division). Keep the decimal point in the answer above the point in the number.
Check: answer × divisor should give the number (12.6 × 0.6 = 7.56 ✓), and the answer should be close to your estimate.

blocks.text: **Big idea:** dividing by a number **between 0 and 1 makes the answer bigger** (18 ÷ 0.4 = 45, which is more than 18). That is because you are asking 'how many 0.4s fit into 18?' — and lots of small pieces fit.

blocks.title: القاعدة اللي لازم تحفظها
blocks.text: الضرب: اضرب من غير العلامة العشرية، وبعدين عدّ الخانات العشرية في السؤال كله وحطها في الناتج. القسمة على عدد عشري: اضرب الرقمين في 10 لحد ما المقسوم عليه يبقى عدد صحيح، وبعدين اقسم عادي. وقبل أي حاجة: قدّر الناتج الأول.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Write these numbers in order, starting with the smallest:  0.65   −0.6   2/5   −3/4   −0.06   [2]

items: Change the fractions to decimals: 2/5 = 0.4 and −3/4 = −0.75.
Negatives first. Their sizes without signs are 0.6, 0.75, 0.06. The biggest of these (0.75) gives the smallest number: −0.75 < −0.6 < −0.06.
Positives next: 0.4 < 0.65.
Write the answer in the **original form**: **−3/4,  −0.6,  −0.06,  2/5,  0.65**

blocks.text: Common mistake: putting −0.06 first because '6 hundredths looks smallest'. −0.06 is very close to zero, so it is the biggest negative. Another mistake: writing the decimals (−0.75, 0.4) instead of the numbers you were given.
**Worked example 2** — Write one of the symbols =, ≠, <, > in each box.  (a) −0.45 ☐ −0.5   (b) 3/8 ☐ 0.375   (c) 7/9 ☐ 0.78   [3]

items: (a) −0.45 is closer to zero than −0.50, so **−0.45 > −0.5**.
(c) 7/9 = 0.7777…, and 0.7777… < 0.7800, so **7/9 < 0.78** (≠ would also be true, but < gives more information; read what the question asks).

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — (a) Estimate 3.6 × 1.25.  (b) Work out 3.6 × 1.25 exactly. Show your working.  [3]

items: (a) 3.6 ≈ 4 and 1.25 ≈ 1, so the estimate is 4 × 1 = **4**.
Decimal places: 3.6 has 1, 1.25 has 2 → 3 in total. 4500 → 4.500.
Answer: **4.5**. Check: close to the estimate 4 ✓.

blocks.text: Common mistake: removing the zeros first (4500 → 45) and then counting 3 places to get 0.045. Count the decimal places **before** you remove the end zeros.
**Worked example 4** — You are told that 23 × 47 = 1081. Use this to write down the answers to (a) 2.3 × 4.7  (b) 0.23 × 470  (c) 10.81 ÷ 2.3  [3]

items: (a) 2.3 × 4.7: two decimal places in total → **10.81**.
(c) Division is the inverse: since 2.3 × 4.7 = 10.81, then 10.81 ÷ 2.3 = **4.7**.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Work out 7.56 ÷ 0.6. Show your working.  [2]

items: Estimate: 7.2 ÷ 0.6 = 72 ÷ 6 = 12, so the answer is about 12.
Short division: 6 into 7 = 1 r 1; 6 into 15 = 2 r 3; decimal point; 6 into 36 = 6. So 75.6 ÷ 6 = 12.6.

blocks.text: Common mistake: multiplying only the divisor by 10 (7.56 ÷ 6 = 1.26). You must change **both** numbers in the same way.
**Worked example 6** — A shop has 9.3 kg of rice. It packs the rice into bags of 0.6 kg.  (a) How many full bags can it make?  (b) How much rice is left over?  [3]

items: (a) 9.3 ÷ 0.6 = 93 ÷ 6 = 15.5. Only **full** bags count, so the answer is **15 bags** (do not round up to 16 — there is not enough rice for a 16th bag).
(b) 15 bags use 15 × 0.6 = 9 kg. Left over: 9.3 − 9 = **0.3 kg**.
Exam technique: in a real-life question, always ask 'does my answer make sense?' — a decimal number of bags is not a final answer.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking −0.8 > −0.08 because 8 tenths is 'more'. On the number line −0.8 is further left, so −0.8 < −0.08.
Thinking a longer decimal is always bigger: 0.507 is less than 0.57.
Writing 0.4 × 0.03 = 0.12. Count the decimal places: 1 + 2 = 3, so 0.012.
Removing end zeros too early: 0.8 × 0.5 → 40 → 2 d.p. → 0.40 = 0.4 (not 0.04).
When dividing, changing only one number: 18 ÷ 0.4 is 180 ÷ 4, not 18 ÷ 4.
Believing 'multiplying always makes bigger' and 'dividing always makes smaller'. With numbers between 0 and 1 it is the opposite.
Using < when the numbers are equal. If they are equal, only =, ≤ or ≥ can be correct.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: 'Write these in order of size, starting with the smallest' — a mix of negative decimals and fractions. Write the final answer using the numbers exactly as given.
'Write <, > or = in the box' or 'Draw a ring around the correct symbol'. Convert fractions to decimals in the margin first.
'Tick (✓) to show whether each statement is true or false', e.g. 0.6 ≥ 3/5. Remember ≥ is true for equal numbers.
'Use the fact that 34 × 56 = 1904 to work out…' — no long calculation is needed; just place the decimal point and check with an estimate.
'Estimate…' — show the rounded numbers you used (e.g. 7 × 4 = 28). An exact calculation does not get the estimation mark.
Paper 1 is non-calculator, so multiplying and dividing decimals by hand is tested there. 'Show your working' means write the whole-number calculation and the decimal-place count.
Word problems (money, lengths, masses): give the unit and round sensibly — money to 2 d.p. ($16.10), 'full bags' down, 'buses needed' up.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Decimals — practice quiz
blocks.intro: Paper 1 style: no calculator. Write your working on paper, then type the answer. Use the minus sign for negative numbers.

questions.e: All are negative, so the largest is the one closest to zero. Sizes without signs: 0.30, 0.31, 0.29, 0.40. The smallest of these is 0.29, so −0.29 is the largest number.

questions.q:
Hana says, 'Multiplying always makes a number bigger, so 8 × 0.4 must be more than 8.'
Explain why Hana is wrong and give the correct value of 8 × 0.4.
questions.ms: 1 mark: explanation that multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 (less than 1) makes the answer smaller, oe (e.g. 0.4 is less than one whole, so you get less than one lot of 8; 8 × 0.4 means 4 tenths of 8). 1 mark: 3.2 cao. Do not accept just 'she is wrong' without a reason.
questions.e: 0.4 is less than 1, so 8 × 0.4 is less than one whole lot of 8. 8 × 0.4 = 8 × 4 ÷ 10 = 32 ÷ 10 = 3.2, which is smaller than 8.

questions.q:
Fabric costs $4.60 per metre. Laila buys 3.5 metres.
Work out the total cost in dollars.
Which of these is the smallest?
questions.e: Change all to decimals: −4/3 = −1.333…, −1.33, −1.3, −1 3/10 = −1.3. Without signs: 1.333… is the biggest, so −4/3 is the smallest. (Note −1.3 = −1 3/10.)

blocks.title: Remember
items: To compare: same number of decimal places, then compare from the left. Change fractions to decimals first.
For negatives, further from zero = smaller: −0.75 < −0.6 < −0.06.
≤ and ≥ include 'equal'; < and > do not; ≠ means 'not equal'.
Multiply decimals: ignore the points, multiply, then the answer has as many decimal places as the question in total.
Divide by a 1 d.p. number: multiply both numbers by 10, then use short division.
Always estimate first and check at the end. × by a number less than 1 → smaller; ÷ by a number less than 1 → bigger.
